passage: In their shared flat in Pune, Lakshmi watched her flatmate Nilesh list his two-year-old phone online for thirty thousand rupees. "That's what it's worth," he said. "I took really good care of it." The first buyer, Sangeeta from the next building, offered fifteen. Nilesh looked insulted. Three more offers came in: fourteen, sixteen, fifteen. "They're all lowballing," he said. Lakshmi pulled up a site selling new phones. "Would you buy your own phone today for thirty?" she asked. "A new one of the next model is thirty-two." Nilesh opened his mouth, then closed it. "No," he admitted. "I wouldn't."

qa.q: What was the price of a new phone of the next model?
qa.a: A new one of the next model was thirty-two.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh feel insulted by Sangeeta's offer of fifteen?
qa.a: The phone is his and he took good care of it, so it feels worth much more to him than to any buyer.

qa.q: Why was Lakshmi's question a useful check?
qa.a: Asking whether he would buy his own phone today for thirty made him look at it as a buyer does, which showed his price was too high.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see the price of thirty thousand?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably sees it as unrealistic for a two-year-old phone, and fifteen as a fair offer rather than a lowball.

grounding: Shows a flatmate seeing a seller price his used phone far above buyers' offers and asking whether he would pay that price today.

"Twenty-five thousand," Hemant said at the office canteen table, tapping his old phone. "Final."
"For that?" Sangeeta asked. "I saw the same model online for twelve."
"Those are beaten up. Mine's special. Never dropped once."
Gopika, his flatmate, stirred her tea. "Hemant, how many people have messaged you?"
"Six."
"And their offers?"
"Eleven, twelve, thirteen... all cheapskates."
"Okay. Question. If Sangeeta was selling her identical phone for twenty-five, would you buy it?"
Hemant frowned. "Hers? No way. I'd pay maybe thirteen."
Gopika raised her eyebrows and said nothing.
Sangeeta grinned. "So... thirteen?"
Hemant sighed. "Fine. Fourteen."

qa.q: How many people had messaged Hemant?
qa.a: Six people had messaged him.

qa.q: Why does Hemant call the buyers cheapskates?
qa.a: His phone feels special to him because it is his and was never dropped, so offers that match the market feel insultingly low.

qa.q: Why did Gopika's question work so quickly?
qa.a: It asked Hemant to be the buyer of an identical phone, and his own answer, thirteen, showed him the gap between owner and buyer.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when Hemant agrees to fourteen?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably feels amused and satisfied, getting a fair price after Hemant's own answer undid his first demand. 😄

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing a seller price his phone far above what buyers offer and asking whether he would pay that price himself.

passage: Last year I learned a lot about value from my flatmate Sumit, though he didn't mean to teach me. I'm Urmila. When he upgraded, he put his old phone up for sale at twenty-two thousand. Buyers came, looked, and offered ten, eleven. He was genuinely hurt. "They don't see how well it works," he told me. One evening I asked, "If you were buying a used phone today, what would you pay for this exact model?" He checked listings for twenty minutes, frowned, and said, "Eleven, maybe twelve." He sold it that weekend for twelve. What stayed with me was how honest he was once he looked at it from the other side.

qa.q: What did Sumit first ask for his old phone?
qa.a: Sumit put it up for sale at twenty-two thousand.

qa.q: Why was Sumit genuinely hurt by the offers?
qa.a: Owning the phone made it feel worth more to him, so buyers' fair offers felt like they didn't see its value.

qa.q: What check did Urmila suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Urmila asked what he would pay for that model as a buyer today, which made him check listings and find the fair price himself.

qa.q: How does Urmila see Sumit's change?
qa.a: Urmila admires how honest he became once he looked at the phone from a buyer's side.

grounding: Shows a flatmate watching a seller price his used phone well above buyers' offers and using the question of what he would pay to close the gap.

passage:
Note in the flat's shared notebook. Written by Asif, Karthik's flatmate and team lead, Sunday.
Karthik put his three-year-old phone up for sale this week for twenty-two thousand. Buyers offered nine, ten, eleven at most. He was annoyed each time. "They don't get it. The camera's still good, and I've taken such care of it." I didn't argue about the price. Instead I asked him, "If you walked into a shop today and saw this exact phone, same scratches, same battery, would you pay twenty-two for it?" He opened his mouth to say yes, then stopped. "No. I'd pay maybe twelve." He looked a bit sheepish. What I did next: I showed him three similar listings, all under thirteen. He dropped his price to twelve that evening. I've noticed I do the same with my old bike, so this note is for me too.

qa.q: What price did Karthik first put on his phone?
qa.a: Twenty-two thousand.

qa.q: Why did Karthik feel buyers "don't get it"?
qa.a: Karthik felt annoyed because, after three years of taking care of the phone, it seemed worth more to him than to anyone else. He saw value in its history that buyers didn't.

qa.q: What question did Asif ask, and why did it work better than arguing?
qa.a: Whether Karthik would pay twenty-two for the same phone in a shop today. It let Karthik look at the price as a buyer and reach the answer himself.

qa.q: How might the buyers have felt when Karthik rejected their offers?
qa.a: They probably felt the price was unrealistic and moved on to cheaper listings.

grounding: A flatmate notes a seller pricing his used phone far above offers, and helps him check whether he would pay that price today.

passage:
Thursday night
Our flatmate Devesh has been trying to sell his old phone for two weeks. He's asking eighteen thousand. Kavitha and I looked it up: the same model, used, sells for around eight. Tonight a buyer came over, a college student with exact cash. She offered nine. Devesh looked offended. "Nine? It still has the original box!" The student left. Kavitha whispered to me, "He'd never pay eighteen for it himself." So after dinner I asked him, gently, "Devesh, if you were buying this today, what would you pay?" He was quiet for a long time, turning the phone over. "Honestly? Ten." Then he laughed at himself a little. "Why does it feel worth more when it's mine?" I didn't have an answer. He's relisting it at ten tomorrow. I wrote this down because I have a whole shelf of old stuff I think is priceless too.
Shalini

qa.q: How much did the college student offer for the phone?
qa.a: She offered nine.

qa.q: Why did Devesh look offended at an offer of nine?
qa.a: As the owner, he valued the phone far above what buyers pay, remembering its box and care. The student's fair offer felt like an insult to him.

qa.q: What question did Shalini ask, and how did it change Devesh's price?
qa.a: "If you were buying this today, what would you pay?" Answering as a buyer, Devesh said ten and decided to relist it at that price.

qa.q: How might the college student have felt when Devesh turned down nine?
qa.a: She may have felt confused or annoyed, having come with exact cash for a fair price, and simply left.

grounding: A flatmate's diary records a seller pricing his old phone far above offers, and a question about what he would pay today.
